rungs.stem: The day after John the Baptist first pointed him out at the Jordan, Jesus met a young man from Bethsaida -- the same fishing town as Peter and Andrew -- and called him with two words: 'Follow me.' Which of the Twelve was this?
rungs.context: John 1:43-44 KJV: 'The day following Jesus would go forth into Galilee, and findeth Philip, and saith unto him, Follow me. Now Philip was of Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.'

rungs.stem: Just after being called by Jesus, Philip ran to find a friend and told him excitedly, 'We have found him, of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, did write -- Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.' What was the friend's name in John's gospel?
rungs.context: John 1:45 KJV. John's gospel alone gives this recruiting scene, and John is the only gospel that uses the name Nathanael.

rungs.stem: Philip's friend was not impressed at all with the news that a Messiah had turned up from a nowhere village in the hills. What was his sceptical one-liner in reply?
choices: Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?
Is not this the carpenter's son from up the road?
Who among the prophets ever came from Galilee?
Why hearken to a man of no name and no city?
rungs.answer: Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?
rungs.context: John 1:46 KJV. Nazareth was a small, undistinguished village in the Galilean hills. Nathanael's opening line reads as the friendly sneer of a man from a slightly better-known town at the news that his neighbour has produced a prophet.

rungs.stem: Philip did not argue with his friend's Nazareth jibe. Instead he gave a three-word invitation that has become one of the most-quoted lines in the whole gospel of John. What did Philip say?
rungs.context: John 1:46 KJV. The phrase is often preached as a model of quiet witness -- no dispute, no proof, just an invitation to look.

rungs.stem: As the sceptical friend walked up, Jesus greeted him with a compliment from across the way: 'Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no...' -- what?
rungs.context: John 1:47 KJV. 'Guile' means deceit or cunning -- Jesus is calling him a straightforward, honest man. Given his blunt Nazareth remark a moment before, the reader has just seen the trait for themselves.

rungs.stem: Startled that this stranger seemed to know him, Nathanael asked, 'Whence knowest thou me?' Jesus answered that he had seen him before Philip ever fetched him -- in a particular spot. Where does Jesus say he saw Nathanael?
rungs.context: John 1:48 KJV: 'Before that Philip called thee, when thou wast under the fig tree, I saw thee.' The fig tree in Jewish tradition was a place of study and prayer -- 'every man under his vine and under his fig tree' (Micah 4:4).

rungs.stem: Won over on the spot by that one detail, Nathanael answered Jesus with a two-part confession -- naming him both a son and a king. What was his declaration?
choices: Rabbi, thou art the Son of God; thou art the King of Israel
My Lord and my God, blessed art thou among prophets
Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God
Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he that cometh
rungs.answer: Rabbi, thou art the Son of God; thou art the King of Israel
rungs.context: John 1:49 KJV. Compare Peter's later confession at Caesarea Philippi (Matthew 16:16) -- Nathanael's has the same substance but comes on his very first meeting.

rungs.stem: Three of the four gospels never mention Nathanael by name at all -- but they do list a disciple always paired with Philip in the roll of the Twelve, whom later Christian tradition identifies as the same man. What is Nathanael's name in Matthew, Mark, and Luke?
rungs.context: Matthew 10:3, Mark 3:18, Luke 6:14. 'Bartholomew' is a patronymic -- Bar-Tolmai, 'son of Talmai' -- a family name rather than a given one, which is why tradition reads Nathanael Bar-Tolmai as a single man with a first name plus a surname.
